subject: anatomy
title: Upper and lower limb nerve injuries and clinical deformities

steps.tx: Peripheral **nerve injuries** produce predictable motor deficits, sensory loss and distinctive deformities based on anatomical innervation. Seddon classified nerve injuries into three grades: neuropraxia with focal conduction block and intact axon; axonotmesis with axonal severance and intact endoneurium; and neurotmesis with complete structural transection requiring surgical repair. Axonal regeneration occurs at approximately one millimeter per day.

steps.tx: The **radial nerve** is vulnerable in mid-shaft humeral fractures within the spiral groove. Injury paralyses the brachioradialis and wrist and finger extensors, causing wrist drop. In the axilla, crutch palsy paralyses the triceps as well. Sensation is lost over the first dorsal web space and anatomical snuffbox. Posterior interosseous nerve injury spares the extensor carpi radialis longus, so wrist extension is preserved without wrist drop.

steps.tx: The **ulnar paradox** states that a high ulnar nerve lesion at the elbow produces a less severe claw hand than a low lesion at the wrist. In high lesions, the flexor digitorum profundus to the fourth and fifth digits is denervated, so the distal interphalangeal joints cannot flex, reducing clawing. In low lesions at Guyon canal, long flexors remain functional, causing pronounced clawing of the ring and little fingers.
steps.say: The ulnar paradox states that a high ulnar nerve lesion at the elbow produces less clawing than a low lesion at the wrist. In high lesions, the flexor digitorum profundus to digits four and five is paralysed, so distal joints do not flex. In low wrist lesions, long flexors remain functional, causing pronounced claw deformity.

steps.tx: The **common fibular nerve** winds around the neck of the fibula, making it the most frequently injured lower limb nerve. Blunt trauma, tight casting or fibular neck fracture causes foot drop due to paralysis of the anterior and lateral compartment leg muscles. The patient adopts a characteristic high-stepping gait to clear the toes during the swing phase, with loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot.
steps.say: The common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, making it the most frequently injured lower limb nerve. Trauma, tight casting or fibular fracture causes foot drop due to paralysis of dorsiflexors and everters. The patient adopts a high-stepping gait, with loss of sensation over the foot dorsum.
